qs.q: An infant presents with jaundice persisting beyond the first 2 weeks of life alongside laboratory signs of cholestatic disease. Which imaging study is specifically warranted to investigate extrahepatic biliary atresia?
o: Radionuclide liver scan for HIDA uptake
qs.e: A radionuclide liver scan for uptake of hepatoiminodiacetic acid (HIDA) is indicated if extrahepatic biliary atresia is suspected. Ultrasonography is also warranted for signs of cholestatic disease.

qs.q: A 3-week-old infant presents with persistent neonatal jaundice. Which clinical finding supports a diagnosis of biliary atresia?
o: Clear urine and normal dark stool
Dark urine and pale clay-colored stool
Absence of jaundice and dark stool
qs.e: Biliary atresia causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which presents with dark urine from renal bilirubin excretion and pale clay-colored stool from absent stercobilin. Clear urine with dark stool indicates unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

faq.a: Phototherapy only converts unconjugated bilirubin; BA produces conjugated bilirubin that cannot be photoconverted.
faq.q: Why does phototherapy not improve jaundice in biliary atresia?

faq.a: It may show bile duct proliferation and fibrosis but is not definitive; cholangiography remains the gold standard.
faq.q: Can a liver biopsy diagnose biliary atresia?

faq.a: Evidence is mixed; some centres give short‑course steroids to reduce inflammation, but routine use is not universally recommended.
faq.q: What is the role of steroids after Kasai surgery?

exam: A 3‑week‑old infant has persistent jaundice, dark urine and pale stools. What is your immediate diagnostic plan and why? — Order LFTs, GGT, ultrasound; if gallbladder not seen, arrange HIDA or refer for cholangiography to rule out BA.
How does the age at Kasai portoenterostomy influence outcome? — Surgery before 60 days yields higher bile flow rates and lower need for transplant; after 90 days success drops dramatically.

Explain why conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in BA does not respond to phototherapy. — Phototherapy only acts on unconjugated bilirubin; conjugated bilirubin is water‑soluble and already excreted via bile.

What are the key differences on ultrasound between biliary atresia and neonatal hepatitis? — BA often shows absent or small gallbladder and intra‑hepatic duct dilatation; hepatitis shows normal gallbladder and no ductal dilatation.

A child post‑Kasai develops fever, abdominal pain and rising bilirubin. What is the likely complication and how do you manage it? — Suspect cholangitis; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, obtain cultures, and consider urgent re‑exploration if no response.

Why are fat‑soluble vitamins essential in the early management of biliary atresia? — Cholestasis impairs absorption of vitamins A, D, E, K, leading to rickets, night‑blindness, coagulopathy; supplementation prevents these sequelae.

In a low‑resource setting without HIDA, how would you proceed when ultrasound is inconclusive? — Refer for intra‑operative cholangiography or early surgical exploration; do not delay surgery awaiting unavailable tests.
What long‑term monitoring is required after a successful Kasai procedure? — Serial LFTs, growth assessment, ultrasound for portal hypertension, and early transplant referral if bile flow declines.
ai.title: Biliary Atresia
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Biliary atresia is a progressive fibro‑obliterative disease of the extra‑hepatic bile ducts presenting with conjugated neonatal jaundice. Early recognition and timely Kasai portoenterostomy are essential to prevent irreversible liver damage.

b: Conjugated bilirubin >20 µmol/L (or direct >20% of total) is abnormal
Absence of gallbladder on ultrasound or non‑visualisation of extra‑hepatic ducts raises suspicion
sections.p: A neonate with persistent conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (>14 days), pale stools and dark urine should be evaluated for biliary atresia after excluding sepsis and metabolic causes.

t.b: Does the gallbladder appear and are the intra‑hepatic ducts dilated? – Non‑visualised gallbladder or ductal dilatation supports BA.
Is there hepatic uptake without excretion into the intestine? – Positive uptake with no excretion suggests extra‑hepatic obstruction.
Is there continuity of the extra‑hepatic biliary tree? – Definitive diagnosis; absence confirms BA.

b: Stage I: Inflammation of the porta hepatis
Stage II: Fibrosis with some ductular remnants
Stage III: Complete obliteration and cirrhosis
sections.p: The Kasai portoenterostomy outcome depends on the age at surgery; earlier (<60 days) yields better bile flow and survival.

b: Idiopathic fibro‑obliteration (most common)
Perinatal viral infections (CMV, hepatitis B)
Associated congenital anomalies (e.g., polysplenia, situs inversus)
Tropical infections (malaria, schistosomiasis) may mimic but are rare causes
sections.p: The exact aetiology is unknown; most cases are idiopathic, but viral, inflammatory and genetic triggers are recognised.

b: Jaundice persisting >2 weeks with direct fraction >20 %
Stool colour: pale/white
Urine colour: dark brown
Hepatomegaly without splenomegaly early; later may develop ascites
sections.p: Typical presentation is a well‑appearing infant with jaundice that does not respond to phototherapy, acholic stools, and dark urine.
Use a stepwise approach: basic labs, imaging, then definitive cholangiography.

t.b: What is the pattern of bilirubin and enzymes? – Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with mildly raised GGT points to cholestasis.
Is GGT markedly elevated (>300 U/L)? – High GGT favours extra‑hepatic obstruction such as BA.
Are the gallbladder and ducts visualised? – Non‑visualisation supports BA; if unavailable, proceed to HIDA or refer.
Does tracer reach intestine? – No excretion suggests BA; if unavailable, arrange early surgical exploration.
Is there continuity of the biliary tree? – Definitive diagnosis; guides immediate Kasai surgery.

b: Rapidly rising bilirubin despite antibiotics
Development of ascites or splenomegaly
Failure to thrive or growth faltering
Bleeding diathesis from coagulopathy
sections.p: If untreated, progressive fibrosis leads to cirrhosis, portal hypertension and liver failure.

b: Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of age – restores bile flow
Fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) supplementation – prevents rickets and night‑blindness
Antibiotic prophylaxis for cholangitis (e.g., amoxicillin‑clavulanate) – treat infections promptly
sections.p: Urgent surgical referral for Kasai portoenterostomy is the cornerstone; supportive care bridges the gap.

t.b: What is the next step? – Arrange transfer to a centre with paediatric hepatobiliary surgery; meanwhile optimise nutrition and vitamins.

b: Liver enzymes and bilirubin every 3 months
Growth charts at each clinic visit
Screen for portal hypertension (ultrasound, platelet count)
Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring for liver function, growth and complications is required; early transplant referral if Kasai fails.

b: Neonatal hepatitis (viral, metabolic) – usually improves with supportive care, no obstructive pattern on imaging
Choledochal cyst – cystic dilatation visible on ultrasound
Alagille syndrome – associated cardiac and vertebral anomalies, paucity of intra‑hepatic ducts
sections.p: Conditions that also cause conjugated neonatal jaundice.

b: Normal GGT early in disease can occur; do not exclude BA on a single value
Ultrasound may miss a tiny gallbladder; combine with HIDA or cholangiography
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring.
